name: Kings Canyon National Park
tagline: Sequoia groves, high Sierra vistas and a glacier-carved canyon of granite walls.

photo.alt: Zumwalt Meadow beneath the granite walls of Kings Canyon
photo.title: Kings Canyon National Park, Zumwalt Meadows
photo.caption: Zumwalt Meadow in Cedar Grove

intro: Kings Canyon has two faces. At Grant Grove, the General Grant Tree, the Nation's Christmas Tree, rises among giant sequoias, and Panoramic Point looks out across the High Sierra. An hour's drive below, the Kings River runs through Cedar Grove between towering granite walls, past meadows and waterfalls. A final adventure here can be a quiet walk among the big trees, a view that seems to take in the whole range, or a long day on the trail to a thundering cascade.
scatterSummary: Scattering is allowed without a permit under the parks' published conditions, at least 100 yards from trails, roads, developed facilities and water.
scatterFacts: No permit is required, according to the parks' Ash Scattering page and the Superintendent's Compendium (36 CFR 2.62(b)). All park regulations still apply.
It should be a small private activity, held away from high visitor-use areas.
Remains must have been processed by pulverization after cremation.
On the ground: at least 100 yards from any trail, road, developed facility or body of water.
From the air: at least 2,000 feet above ground level, and not over developed areas, facilities or bodies of water.
No markers or memorials, and no publicity may be given to the activity.
scatterNotes: The parks' Permits & Reservations page still lists ash scattering among activities that need a special use permit, while the Ash Scattering page (updated February 25, 2026) and the Superintendent's Compendium say no permit is required. Call the park to confirm before your trip.
beforeYouGo: Highway 180 enters Kings Canyon National Park from Fresno at the Big Stump Entrance; it is the preferred route for longer vehicles. Highway 180 from Grant Grove to Cedar Grove is open seasonally, generally from the fourth Friday in April to mid-November, and much of it runs through Sequoia National Forest. Cedar Grove is about an hour's drive from the Kings Canyon Visitor Center. Tire chains may be required any time it snows, and there are no gas stations in the parks. Road conditions: 559-565-3341.

destinations.name: General Grant Tree

photo.alt: The General Grant Tree in Grant Grove, Kings Canyon National Park

destinations.description: The General Grant Tree is the second-largest tree in the world, and it carries two more titles: the Nation's Christmas Tree and the country's only living national shrine. A paved loop leads through the Grant Grove to its base, past the historic Gamlin Cabin and the Fallen Monarch, a sequoia you can walk inside. Benches wait at pullouts along the way, so there is time to sit together beneath its 268-foot crown and simply be with one another.

plan.distance: 0.5 mi loop (1/3 mi on the park's day hikes page)
plan.accessibility: Paved, with steep sections; not designated wheelchair accessible. Tactile panels with Braille, benches at pullouts, and limited accessible parking (NPS)
plan.bestTime: Year-round; snowshoes may be needed when icy
plan.scattering: Not at this spot; no permit needed away from it (see below)

drive.route: Highway 180 through the Big Stump Entrance to Grant Grove, then one mile north of the Kings Canyon Visitor Center on Grant Tree Road to the General Grant parking lot.

trail.name: General Grant Tree Trail
steps: From the parking lot, follow the paved loop through the Grant Grove.
Pass the Fallen Monarch and the Gamlin Cabin on the way around.
A short side trail around the tree itself includes stairs; it can be bypassed to complete the loop.

scatterNote.text: No permit is needed, but scatter on the ground at least 100 yards from any trail, road, developed facility or body of water, away from busy areas such as this grove. Pulverized remains only; no markers, memorials or publicity.

destinations.name: Panoramic Point

photo.alt: View from Panoramic Point over forested ridges toward Hume Lake and the Sierra
photo.title: Výhled z Panoramic Point na jezero Hume Lake - panoramio

destinations.description: From Panoramic Point you look across hundreds of miles of Kings Canyon and the neighboring forest lands. Hume Lake sits far below, and beyond it the deep glacial gorge of Kings Canyon opens toward a skyline of High Sierra peaks. Artists, poets and early leaders of the national park idea all spent time on these heights. Bring a thermos and a few photographs, and let the family take in a view wide enough to hold a whole lifetime of memories.

plan.distance: Half-mile accessible trail to the viewing area
plan.difficulty: Moderate slope: an accessible path with cross slopes that may be difficult for some (NPS)
plan.accessibility: Accessible trail, accessible parking stall, restrooms and picnic tables (NPS)
plan.bestTime: In winter, the trailhead is reached only on foot, snowshoes or skis
plan.scattering: Not at this spot; no permit needed away from it (see below)

drive.route: From the Kings Canyon Visitor Center in Grant Grove, a short drive up Panoramic Point Road. The road is narrow and twisting with blind curves, RVs and oversized vehicles are prohibited, and parking is very limited.

points.label: Restrooms at the Panoramic Point trailhead area

trail.name: Panoramic Point trail
steps: Walk the half-mile path up to the viewing area.
For more, continue on a more difficult 2.6-mile unpaved hike to the Park Ridge Fire Lookout.

scatterNote.text: No permit is needed, but scatter on the ground at least 100 yards from any trail, road, developed facility or body of water, so not at the viewing area itself. Pulverized remains only; no markers, memorials or publicity.

destinations.name: Roaring River Falls

photo.alt: Roaring River Falls pouring through a granite chute into a pool
photo.title: Roaring River Falls, Kings Canyon National Park

destinations.description: Roaring River travels down from deep wilderness canyons and crashes through a narrow granite chute into a pool, and on a warm day the falling water stirs up its own cool breeze. A short, shady, paved walk brings the whole family to the spray, where mist swirls up into the treetops. Stand together by the water, let its sound fill the quiet, and take a moment to remember. Those who want to walk on can follow the River Trail toward Zumwalt Meadow.

plan.distance: About 0.5 mi from the parking lot
plan.accessibility: Paved and relatively accessible; the paving was improved and the steepest grades reduced in 2017 (NPS)
plan.bestTime: Biggest and loudest in late spring and early summer; Highway 180 to Cedar Grove is closed in winter
plan.scattering: Not at this spot; no permit needed away from it (see below)

drive.route: Highway 180 to Cedar Grove, about an hour's drive from the Kings Canyon Visitor Center, then 3 miles east of Cedar Grove Village to the small Roaring River trailhead lot. Overflow parking is across the bridge.

trail.name: Roaring River Falls trail
steps: Follow the short, shaded, paved path to the falls viewpoint.
Optional: the River Trail junction is a few feet from the trail toward the parking area; a 3.9-mile round-trip lollipop leads to Zumwalt Meadow.
notes: The rocks are slippery, and currents under the calm-looking pool can be deadly. Stay out of the water.

scatterNote.text: No permit is needed, but scatter on the ground at least 100 yards from any trail, road, developed facility or body of water, so not at the falls or along the river. Pulverized remains only; no markers, memorials or publicity.

destinations.name: Mist Falls

photo.alt: Mist Falls tumbling over granite in the South Fork Canyon of the Kings River
photo.title: Mist Falls, Kings Canyon National Park

destinations.description: From Road's End, the trail to Mist Falls follows the glaciated South Fork Canyon through forest and chaparral, past a long show of rapids and cascades, to one of the largest waterfalls in the two parks. It is a full day on foot, mostly gentle until the last wooded mile, and that steady walking side by side leaves plenty of room for conversation. At the falls, find a safe, dry rock well back from the spray and share the stories you came to tell.

plan.difficulty: Not rated by NPS (no Easy, Moderate or Strenuous label published); an all-day walk, relatively flat until the last mile
plan.accessibility: Sandy trail; not wheelchair accessible. Accessible parking at Road's End (NPS)
plan.bestTime: Highway 180 to Cedar Grove typically reopens the fourth Friday in April and closes mid-November
plan.scattering: Not at this spot; no permit needed away from it (see below)

drive.route: Highway 180 to Cedar Grove, about an hour's drive from the Kings Canyon Visitor Center, then to the end of the highway at Road's End. Start at the trailhead just past the Road's End Permit Station.

points.label: Woods Creek and Bubbs Creek Trailhead

trail.name: Woods Creek Trail to Mist Falls
steps: Start at the trailhead just past the Road's End Permit Station.
At the first trail junction, about two miles from Road's End, take the trail on the left.
Climb the last wooded mile, about 600 ft, to the falls.
notes: Mist and spray make the rocks slippery and treacherous; people have slipped and fallen here. River currents can drag you under. Kings Canyon is a very active bear area: use the food storage lockers.

scatterNote.text: No permit is needed, but scatter on the ground at least 100 yards from any trail, road, developed facility or body of water, so not at the falls or along this riverside trail. Pulverized remains only; no markers, memorials or publicity.
